programme.title: AI Engineering
programme.subtitle: An indie degree
programme.framing_note: Degree-rigorous internally — blocks, credits, prerequisites, capstone. The public artifact is a transcript with evidence tiers and linked artifacts, never a diploma. Rendering is a template choice; nothing here depends on it.
programme.pacing_note: Hours vary week to week. Progress is banked and monotonic — no streaks, nothing destroyable by a quiet month. Projected completion is a range derived from logged hours, never from intended hours.
programme.ordering_principle: Value-weighted within prerequisite constraints. Stopping at any point should leave the highest-value skills already banked, so an unfinished programme is still a gain.
programme.public_log: Every course publishes, but into one growing public engineering log rather than six standalone posts. A reader arrives once and finds a body of work that compounds; six separate write-ups fragment the same effort into things nobody finishes. Each course contributes a chapter that must stand alone on its own page and must also connect backwards to at least one earlier chapter's result.
programme.optional_note: Optional items are duplicates of work an earlier course already required. They are kept rather than deleted, because a second pass is sometimes what makes a thing land — but the programme total counts required work only, and completion never waits for them.
programme.brand_note: Indie Degree is the platform; this instance is an indie MSc in AI engineering. Indie carries the same meaning it does in film and games — produced outside the institution, deliberately, and judged on the work rather than on who signed it off.
programme.capability_note: The unit that matters is not the credit, it is the capability claim — the line you are willing to put in the skills section of a CV and then defend to someone who sets the questions. Areas carry that claim; courses sequence the work that earns it. A claim needs a purpose-built public artifact, a measured result, a documented place where the technique stops working, an unscripted defence, and recall a week later without notes. Four of those can be faked by a diligent afternoon; the negative result and the defence cannot, which is why both are mandatory rather than bonus.

blocks.title: Applied AI Engineering
blocks.purpose: The employable core. Closes the distance to applied and field AI roles, where the gap read already puts the learner at 94%.

blocks.title: Depth
blocks.purpose: What makes this a programme rather than a certificate. Builds the models rather than calling them.

1.name: Machine-verified
1.example: Tests pass, quiz scored, benchmark number reproduced.

2.name: Panel-assessed
2.example: Multiple models score against a rubric registered before submission; disagreement is shown, not averaged.

3.name: Artifact in the world
3.example: Public repo, deployed service, reproducible result, published write-up.

4.name: Defended
4.example: Unscripted spoken answers to questions about your own submission.

areas.name: Engineering foundations
areas.supporting_note: Medium of instruction. Python and deployment are how the work gets done, never what is being claimed — putting them forward as the achievement would misrepresent the programme.

areas.name: Mathematics for machine learning
areas.supporting_note: Load-bearing under deep-learning and fine-tuning, but nobody hires an AI engineer for a linear-algebra line. It earns its place by making other claims defensible.

areas.name: Machine learning foundations
areas.supporting_note: Substrate for evaluation and architecture. The claim it supports is 'I knew a classifier would beat the LLM here', which belongs to architecture.

areas.name: Deep learning
areas.supporting_note: Substrate for transformers and fine-tuning. Claimed through what it enables, not on its own.

areas.name: Text representation
areas.supporting_note: Tokenisation and embeddings are prerequisites for retrieval and transformers. They are a component of those claims rather than a claim of their own.

areas.name: LLM application engineering
areas.claim: I can take a model API to a production feature — structured output that cannot be malformed, tool interfaces a model can actually use, a context budget I chose on purpose, and a hallucination guard that fails closed.

artifact.name: 1 Percent More Fluent
artifact.what: A shipped product whose structured-output path and streaming decisions are documented and defensible.

areas.name: Evaluation and measurement
areas.claim: I can say with a number whether an LLM system is any good, defend the method that produced the number, and show where the measurement itself breaks down.

artifact.name: eval-harness
artifact.what: A replay-first harness with per-tag reporting and a baseline that fails CI on regression, run against a hand-built gold set including negatives.

areas.name: Retrieval and context systems
areas.claim: I can design a retrieval system, measure retrieval separately from generation, and name the corpus properties that decide whether embeddings, lexical search or hybrid wins.

artifact.name: retrieval-bench
artifact.what: Two corpora chosen because they fail differently — dense proper-noun rate documents against near-synonymous prose — with the crossover point where hybrid stops paying for itself.

areas.name: Agents and tool-use systems
areas.claim: I can choose between a workflow and an agent and justify it, sandbox what a model is allowed to touch, and measure multi-step reliability rather than assert it.

artifact.name: agent-vs-workflow
artifact.what: One stage of a working deterministic pipeline rebuilt as an autonomous agent, with the cost, latency and reliability of both measured side by side.

areas.name: Inference, cost and latency
areas.cv_line: LLM inference cost and latency optimisation
areas.claim: I can account for token spend per run, cut time-to-first-token against a stated budget, and say which optimisations were not worth their complexity.

artifact.name: cost-and-latency-study
artifact.what: A streaming product profiled end to end, with a caching and routing change measured against a before baseline rather than estimated.

areas.name: Speech and voice interfaces
areas.claim: I can close a speech loop with a latency budget that survives a real conversation, and handle the case everyone skips — a user interrupting.

artifact.name: voice-loop
artifact.what: A bidirectional speech path with a measured turn-taking budget and a documented barge-in behaviour.

areas.name: Vision-language and documents
areas.claim: I can extract structure from real documents and say where a vision-language model is worse than the boring parser it replaced.

artifact.name: document-extraction
artifact.what: Extraction over genuinely messy source documents, scored against a parser baseline on the same inputs.

areas.name: Safety and adversarial testing
areas.claim: I can red-team a system I built, handle personal data deliberately rather than incidentally, and show the attacks that still work.

artifact.name: red-team-report
artifact.what: An adversarial pass over a live product, with the successful attacks published alongside the mitigations.

areas.name: Architecture and judgement
areas.claim: I can decide whether a problem needs an LLM at all, price the alternative, and show a case where the cheaper approach won.

artifact.name: llm-or-not
artifact.what: A classification problem currently served by an LLM, reimplemented with a baseline that is measured against it on cost, latency and accuracy.

areas.name: Transformer internals
areas.claim: I can implement attention and a transformer block from scratch and explain what each part is for without reciting a diagram.

artifact.name: transformer-from-scratch
artifact.what: A working implementation trained on something small, with the ablations that show which components matter.

areas.name: Fine-tuning and post-training
areas.claim: I can curate training data, run a parameter-efficient fine-tune, and show the case where prompting would have been enough.

artifact.name: fine-tune-study
artifact.what: A fine-tune measured against a well-prompted baseline on the same eval set.

areas.name: Reinforcement learning
areas.claim: I can explain how preference data becomes a policy, and where reward modelling goes wrong.

artifact.name: rlhf-study
artifact.what: A small policy-gradient implementation and a written account of a reward-hacking failure.

skills.name: Python and the numeric stack
skills.note: Medium of instruction, never a learning objective. Evidenced as a byproduct of coursework.

skills.name: Calibrating automated scores to human judgement
Regression testing and CI for models

courses.title: LLM Application Engineering
courses.why: Everything else in Block I assumes you can get reliable, structured, tool-using behaviour out of a model. Four shipped products already evidence most of this.
outcomes: Specify and enforce structured output such that malformed responses are impossible rather than unlikely
Design tool interfaces a model can actually use, and explain why a given interface fails
Name and detect the specific failure modes of a deployed LLM feature
Manage context deliberately — what goes in, what gets dropped, and what that costs

courses.title: Evaluation and Measurement
courses.why: The highest-value and least-practised skill in applied AI, and the one that makes every later claim in this programme defensible. It is also the course that makes Indie Degree's own grading panel credible — you cannot honestly grade with a judge you have not calibrated.
outcomes: Build an eval set from production failures rather than from imagination
Name and measure the known pathologies of LLM judges — position, verbosity, self-enhancement bias
Calibrate an automated judge against your own labels and report the agreement, not just the score
Decide whether a difference between two systems is real, with an interval rather than a vibe
Wire evals into CI so a regression fails a build

courses.title: Retrieval and Context Systems
courses.why: Retrieval is the default answer to most enterprise AI questions and is wrong about a third of the time. Knowing when not to use it is the differentiator.
outcomes: Build hybrid retrieval and show where lexical beats dense, with numbers
Choose a chunking strategy from measured retrieval quality rather than from a blog post
Evaluate retrieval separately from generation, and locate which half is failing
Articulate when long context replaces retrieval and when it does not
Enforce document-level access control through a retrieval pipeline, and prove it holds
courses.advanced_standing_note: Nothing carries over. Carpark SG integrates external data sources but does no embedding retrieval, and none of the four products rank or evaluate retrieved results.

courses.title: Agents and Tool-Use Systems
courses.why: Multi-step reliability is where demos die. Compounding per-step error is an arithmetic problem before it is a prompting one.
outcomes: Derive the reliability of an n-step agent from its per-step success rate, and design against it
Choose between workflow and agent for a given task and defend the choice
Sandbox tool access to least privilege
Evaluate an agent on task completion rather than on transcript plausibility
Red-team your own agent and report what you got it to do that it should not
Justify a multi-agent design against a single-agent baseline, or decline to build one
State what personal data enters a model, where it goes, and what the local regulator expects

courses.title: Inference, Cost and Latency Engineering
courses.why: The questions a field engineer is actually asked in the room: what will this cost at our volume, and how fast will it feel. Very few candidates can answer either with a number.
outcomes: Model the token cost of a feature at a given volume, before building it
Explain the prefill/decode split and what each implies for latency
Apply caching, batching and streaming, and measure what each bought
Read a serving stack — paged attention, continuous batching, quantisation — and reason about its trade-offs
Degrade a model-backed feature gracefully rather than failing it

courses.title: Speech and Multimodal Systems
courses.why: Domain depth for voice AI specifically, where existing shipped work already provides a foundation and the target employers live.
outcomes: Build a full ASR → reasoning → TTS loop and account for every millisecond in the budget
Explain why transport choice dominates perceived latency in voice agents
Measure ASR quality properly, including on accented and code-switched speech
Handle barge-in, turn-taking and partial results
Decide whether a document problem needs vision at all, and show the measurement behind the answer

courses.title: Mathematics for Machine Learning
courses.why: Targeted, not an undergraduate sequence. Only what is needed to read the papers and understand what training is doing.
outcomes: Manipulate matrices, eigendecompositions and projections fluently enough to read architecture papers
Differentiate through a computational graph by hand
Reason about distributions, expectation and variance in a loss function
Explain gradient descent and its common variants from the mathematics, not the metaphor

courses.title: Machine Learning Foundations
courses.why: The classical grounding that makes deep learning legible rather than magical, and the source of most evaluation intuition.
outcomes: Implement linear and logistic regression, and a tree ensemble, from scratch
Diagnose bias and variance from learning curves
Choose and justify a metric for an imbalanced problem
Explain what a model is fitting, and to what

courses.title: Deep Learning
courses.why: Backpropagation built by hand, then the training dynamics that decide whether a network learns anything.
outcomes: Implement reverse-mode autodiff from scratch and use it to train a network
Debug a training run from its loss curve
Apply and justify normalisation, initialisation and regularisation choices
Read an architecture diagram and implement it

courses.title: Transformers and LLMs from Scratch
courses.why: The flagship of Block II. Ends with a working GPT you can explain line by line — the single most legible artifact in the programme.
outcomes: Implement multi-head self-attention from scratch, without reference
Train a small GPT end to end, from tokeniser to sampling
Explain every architectural choice in a modern decoder and what it is buying
Reproduce a published result and account for the gap where you fail to

courses.title: Fine-tuning and Post-training
courses.why: Where a base model becomes a product, and where evaluation discipline from AIE-102 stops being optional.
outcomes: Curate a fine-tuning dataset and defend every inclusion rule
Run LoRA fine-tuning and measure whether it actually helped
Explain preference optimisation and implement DPO
Detect and report regression on capabilities you did not intend to change

courses.title: Reinforcement Learning
courses.why: Lowest immediate employability of the deep track, and the necessary grounding for RLHF and for reasoning-model training. Placed late on purpose.
outcomes: Formalise a problem as an MDP
Implement a value-based and a policy-gradient agent
Explain the credit assignment problem and how RLHF inherits it
Connect policy optimisation to preference optimisation from AIE-205

courses.title: Systems for Machine Learning
courses.why: The hardware reality underneath everything above. Explains why architectures look the way they do.
outcomes: Explain the memory hierarchy of a GPU and why attention is IO-bound
Profile a training step and identify the bottleneck
Describe data, tensor and pipeline parallelism and when each applies
Reason about the arithmetic intensity of an operation

courses.title: Capstone
courses.why: One substantial system that exercises the whole programme, shipped publicly and defended aloud. This is the artifact the transcript is built around.
outcomes: Ship a system that a stranger can use, with published evaluation results
Report honestly on what did not work and what the numbers actually say
Defend the design under unscripted questioning
Write it up so a hiring manager can assess it in ten minutes

courses.title: Architecture and Judgement
courses.why: Every other Block I course teaches you to build one thing well; none asks whether you should have built it. This one does nothing else — rules versus classical ML versus an LLM, decided with measurements, and the human-in-the-loop routing that follows from it.
outcomes: Decide between rules, a classical model and an LLM for a stated problem, and defend it with numbers
Produce and read the classification metrics that decision rests on, including calibration
Set a confidence threshold for human review from data rather than by feel, and state what it costs
Build a model selection matrix, and a build-versus-buy case a finance-literate reader would accept

accepted_inversions.rationale: Applied-first ordering means some skills are used before they are derived. Deliberate: you learn to measure a judge before you can prove the statistics, and to call attention before you can differentiate it. Each pair below is an accepted, recorded exception; anything not listed here is a genuine ordering bug.
